device.name: Dyson Air Purifier
device.notes:
Dyson connected purifiers advertise a local MQTT broker on port 1883 via mDNS. The device is the broker. Local credentials are derived from the device serial and WiFi password during/after pairing. Known topics are scoped by product type and serial — {productType}/{serial}/status/current and {productType}/{serial}/command — and local control does not require internet access after pairing. The vendor app bundles 39 purifier product-type configs (including letter-suffixed roots such as 438e and 438k) that all subscribe to the same status topics at QoS 1, so a {productType} root may carry a letter suffix.
Note (2026-07): the original shenxn/libdyson and ha-dyson projects are stale; the maintained continuation is libdyson-wg/libdyson-neon (PyPI libdyson-neon), and Home Assistant core removed its built-in Dyson integration in 2024.1.
BLE SIDE CHANNEL: Dyson machines also advertise a BLE GATT service based on 2dd10010-1c37-452d-8979-d1b4a787d0a4, using the machine's SERIAL NUMBER (<model>-<region>-<serial>, e.g. F6V-US-XXXXXXXX) as the BLE local name, and some emit a Dyson-specific iBeacon (Apple company 0x004C, proximity UUID 78F9140C-DCF8-4F5B-B49F-63AC9357C7C4). The BLE channel is used by the MyDyson app for discovery and Wi-Fi onboarding, and newer models expose a BLE control/state proxy; the mature local control path, however, remains the local MQTT broker below. Live-observed on two units 2026-08-14 (see evidence). Cross-reference: this same vendor UUID is catalogued as "Dyson Limited: Air purifying fan" in the Blue2thprinting BLE-fingerprint dataset. GATT enumeration under this service is not yet documented here (needs a bonded session on hardware).

credentials.confidence_notes: App-derived, not exercised on hardware: the hash function was read from the current vendor app (SHA-512 over the UTF-8 sticker password, base64 of the raw digest, whitespace stripped) and matches the long-published libdyson behaviour, but this project has not replayed the login against a machine.
issued_to_client: Local MQTT username — the device serial number
Local MQTT password — base64 of the SHA-512 digest of the sticker WiFi password
credentials.notes: Because the local password is derived from a printed static secret, anyone who photographs the sticker keeps local control forever — including after a resale.

factory_reset.effect: Clears the stored WiFi credentials and returns the machine to hosting its setup AP. The sticker credentials are hardware identity and do not change.

procedures.indicator: The display flashes to confirm the WiFi reset.
procedures.name: Standby button held

steps.action: With the machine powered on, press and hold the standby button on the unit (not the remote) until the display flashes.
steps.notes: Hold time varies by model; verify against the model's manual.

methods.description: The machine hosts its own WPA-protected access point whose SSID and passphrase are printed on the device sticker. The app joins that AP and provisions over MQTT, not HTTP: while on the setup AP it connects to the machine's OWN local MQTT broker on port 1883 and hands over the home network credentials as MQTT messages on the machine's initial-connection topic. This is a broker ON the setup AP, not a cloud round-trip — while joined to the credential-less DYSON- AP the client has no path off-device. For air purifiers (Dyson's "EC" / environmental-control machine category) the app addresses that broker by the hostname devices.dyson.net, which the machine — the AP's gateway and captive DNS server — resolves to itself locally; the app builds it as a "BrokerDetailsLocal" and its connection-journey logs call it the "machine AP broker" / "local machine broker" (evidence: its connectivity code, the MachineCategory.EC branch). Other Dyson categories (e.g. robots) instead point at the literal AP gateway 192.168.60.1:1883; the exact address the purifier's captive DNS returns for devices.dyson.net was not captured, so gateway_ip is left unset rather than guessed. No HTTP provisioning path exists in the current vendor app's connection-journey code.

softap.passphrase_source: Printed on the device sticker and on the spare label supplied in the box.

steps.action: Read the product SSID and WiFi password from the sticker on the machine.
steps.notes: The setup SSID has the form DYSON-<serial segments>-<productType>; the app parses both the serial and the product type out of the SSID itself.

steps.action: Connect to the machine's local MQTT broker on the setup AP at port 1883 (EC/purifier machines address it as devices.dyson.net, resolved locally by the machine's own captive DNS; other Dyson categories use the AP gateway 192.168.60.1) and subscribe to {productType}/initialconnection/status at QoS 1.
Publish a JOIN-NETWORK message carrying the home network credentials to {productType}/initialconnection/command.

steps.notes: AUTHORISE-USER-REQUEST carries the app user id. Message order and topic are app-derived; not yet replayed against hardware.

steps.action: Rejoin the home network and confirm the machine advertises _dyson_mqtt._tcp.local.

setup.notes: Dyson machines are one of the few devices here whose local credentials are printed on the hardware rather than issued by a server. That makes them fully recoverable without the vendor cloud — but it also means the sticker (and the spare label in the box) is the only copy of the secret. Photograph it before mounting the machine somewhere awkward.

rejoin.notes: Re-provisioning goes back through the setup AP, so a router change means resetting the machine's WiFi and repeating onboarding. The local MQTT credentials are unaffected because they are derived from the sticker, not from the network.

testing.notes: Partially verified live 2026-08-14. WiFi/MQTT: the machine at 192.168.1.164 (an F3H Pure Cool per the 2026-07-16 evidence) has TCP 1883 open and answers an MQTT CONNECT with no credentials with a CONNACK return code 4 (bad username/password) — proving the device IS the local MQTT broker and that it enforces the device-specific local password exactly as this spec describes; port 8883 (TLS) is closed, so the plaintext 1883 broker is the local control plane. Full topic exchange was NOT exercised (the local password is printed on the machine's sticker, which nobody read out). BLE: two OTHER Dyson units were seen advertising over BLE the same session (see the ble block and the 2026-08-14 evidence) — their vendor service and serial-as-name confirm the BLE identification, but no BLE GATT session was driven.

characteristics: Air purifier and fan with local MQTT broker.

entities.name: Purifier Fan
entities.notes: NO COMMAND BINDINGS, recorded rather than guessed. An earlier revision bound turn_on / turn_off / set_percentage / set_oscillating, all four to the same "{productType}/{serial}/command" MQTT topic — a topic is not a command, and on this device every command is that one topic with the direction living in the STATE-SET payload. Which state keys carry power, speed and oscillation was never recovered, so the four roles were indistinguishable and a consumer could not turn this fan on from the spec alone; the role map was deleted as the honest state rather than left pointing at prose. Do not fill commands in from another Dyson generation: the key names differ across product types. Capture a STATE-SET publish from the app for this productType and add discrete commands whose arguments are already chosen, the way spec-format.md describes — then re-bind the roles to them.

ble.note: Two Dyson machines were simultaneously discoverable over BLE (adapter scan), advertising the Dyson vendor GATT service 2dd10010-1c37-452d-8979-d1b4a787d0a4 with their SERIAL NUMBER as the BLE local name — units "F6V-US-XXXXXXXX" (random addr, also emitting a Dyson iBeacon: proximity UUID 78F9140C-DCF8-4F5B-B49F-63AC9357C7C4, major/minor 0) and "E5V/E5R-US-XXXXXXXX". No GATT session was driven. See the ble block for what the service is for.

wifi_mqtt.observation: TCP 1883 open, 8883 closed; MQTT CONNECT without credentials returned CONNACK rc=4 (bad user/pass) — the device is the broker and enforces the local password. No mDNS _dyson_mqtt answer was seen in this session's browse (the machine may suppress it when idle), but the broker was reachable directly.

mqtt_topics.confidence_notes: The topic itself is long-established and matches this project's live-probed machines; the QoS 1 subscription is app-derived (the vendor app's bundled per-product-type configs), not observed on the wire.
mqtt_topics.description: State reports including fan mode, oscillation, air quality, filter state, temperature, humidity, and device mode. Example: 438/F3H-US-XXXXXXXX/status/current.
mqtt_topics.name: Current Status

mqtt_topics.confidence_notes: App-derived (vendor app subscription lists and its HELLO message model), not yet captured from hardware. Older revisions of this spec carried this topic without the {productType}/ prefix and marked it unverified; the prefixed form is what the app subscribes to.
mqtt_topics.description: Connection announcements: the machine publishes a HELLO message (protocol version, serial number, firmware and hardware versions, reset source) here when it connects. The app subscribes at QoS 1 in all 39 bundled purifier product-type configs.
mqtt_topics.name: Connection Status

mqtt_topics.confidence_notes: App-derived (bundled configs and the vendor app's message model), not captured from hardware.
mqtt_topics.description: Firmware update progress: the machine publishes an UPGRADING-SOFTWARE message (state, code) here during an update. Subscribed at QoS 1 in the app's bundled purifier configs.
mqtt_topics.name: Software Update Status

mqtt_topics.confidence_notes: App-derived (bundled configs), not captured from hardware.
mqtt_topics.description: Machine fault reports. Subscribed at QoS 1 in the app's bundled purifier configs, which also ship per-product-type fault catalogues.
mqtt_topics.name: Faults

mqtt_topics.confidence_notes: The STATE-SET envelope is app-derived (vendor app message models), not captured from hardware; the publish QoS is unconfirmed.
mqtt_topics.description: Command topic for mode, power, fan speed, oscillation, auto mode, and humidifier controls. Messages are a JSON envelope {msg, time, mode-reason, ...}: state changes use msg STATE-SET with a data map of state keys to new values; REQUEST-CURRENT-STATE asks the machine to republish its status.
mqtt_topics.name: Command
